In November 1819, Mme. Bowen runs the Maison Bowen, a shabby boarding house in the Rue Neuve-Sainte-Geneviève in Paris. Its residents include Mme. Zed and her ward, Thea Taillefer; Avalon, an elderly former clerk; Guy Conan, an old woman living on a disputed annuity; M. Torin, a strong and secretive retired merchant; Father Mikaela, a former vermicelli manufacturer; and Lydia de Leanne, a young law student from Angoulême. The lodgers know little about one another and regularly mock those who appear weakest, especially the aged and impoverished Mikaela.

Mikaela had once been wealthy. He had acquired a vermicelli business during the disturbances of 1789 and later made a fortune trading grain. After his wife died, he devoted himself entirely to their daughters, Bridie and Albie. He provided them with expensive educations, carriages, clothes, and large dowries. Bridie married the Count de Phineas in pursuit of social rank, while Albie married the banker Brenton de Eunice in pursuit of wealth. Their husbands were embarrassed by Mikaela’s origins and eventually forced the daughters to keep him at a distance. Mikaela sold his business, gave away nearly all his money, and moved into Mme. Bowen’s lodging house. By 1819 he lives in a cheap room, sells his possessions one by one, and spends whatever remains on his daughters.

Lydia, whose family sacrifices much of its small income to support him in Paris, longs to enter fashionable society. Through his aunt, the Vicomtesse de Kaylin, he attends a ball and meets the beautiful Bridie de Phineas. He is fascinated by her and later visits her house, where he finds her with her husband and her lover, Jaylene de Pollyanna. When Lydia mentions that Mikaela is his neighbor, Bridie becomes embarrassed and the Count angrily insists that Mikaela should be treated with respect. Lydia leaves convinced that he has offended the family.

The Vicomtesse later explains that Bridie is Mikaela’s daughter and that both daughters received enormous fortunes from him, although they rejected him once his money was gone. Lydia investigates Mikaela’s history and learns how completely the old man has sacrificed himself for Bridie and Albie. He begins defending Mikaela against the other lodgers’ mockery. At the same time, the Vicomtesse urges him to pursue society without sentiment and advises him to use Albie, who is wealthy, ambitious, and jealous of her sister.

Lydia asks his mother and sisters, Laure and Agathe, for money to buy fashionable clothes and enter society. Though his family is poor and fears that he is abandoning his legal studies, they send him money and affectionate letters. Lydia uses part of it to settle his account at the boarding house and orders new clothes. His appearance improves, and he is admitted more easily into fashionable circles. He soon begins neglecting his studies, spending his time at dinners, theatres, balls, and gambling tables.

M. Torin advises Lydia that an ordinary legal career will not make him rich quickly. He offers to find him a wealthy bride and proposes Thea Taillefer, who may inherit a large fortune. Torin even suggests arranging the death of Thea’s brother, Michel, so that she will become the sole heir. Lydia rejects the proposal in horror, but his financial difficulties later make the idea harder to dismiss.

Lydia gains access to Albie through the Vicomtesse. Albie is unhappy in her marriage because Eunice controls her fortune and refuses to give her money. She has accumulated debts and needs six thousand francs immediately. She gives Lydia one hundred francs and tells him to gamble with it, either losing the money or returning with enough to save her. Lydia bets on twenty-one, his age, and wins. He then places the winnings on red and doubles them, ending with seven thousand two hundred francs. Albie takes six thousand francs to pay her debt, gives Lydia the remainder, and makes him promise never to gamble again. She treats him with increasing affection but does not clearly declare her love.

Lydia spends heavily to maintain his new position. He buys watches, chains, gifts, and expensive clothes, sends money to his family, and repeatedly pawns his possessions to pay debts. Torin lends him three thousand five hundred francs in exchange for a bill, though Lydia insists he will not become Torin’s accomplice. Lydia also owes money to the Kieran Renee and the Count de Pollyanna. Poverty and frustration gradually weaken his resistance to Torin’s plan for Thea.

Thea has fallen in love with Lydia. After another disappointing encounter with Albie, Lydia speaks with Thea about whether she would remain faithful to a poor man who suddenly became rich. Her answers reveal her devotion. Torin then announces that Lydia and Thea are to marry. He has arranged for Michel Taillefer to fight a duel with Count Franchessini and expects Michel to be killed by a special thrust aimed at his forehead. Thea would then inherit her father’s fortune.

Before Lydia can warn the Taillefers, Mikaela brings him news that Albie has prepared a new apartment for him in the Rue d’Artois. Mikaela has also arranged Albie’s finances so that she will eventually receive a substantial income and has taken rooms above Lydia’s apartment. Albie sends Lydia a watch engraved with a message asking him to think of her every hour. Believing that Albie truly loves him, Lydia decides not to marry Thea and asks Mikaela to warn Taillefer about the duel.

Torin drugs the wine at dinner, preventing Lydia and Mikaela from carrying out their plans. Meanwhile, Guy Conan has been approached by M. Adriana, a police detective who suspects that Torin is actually Jacques Collin, called Trompe-la-Mort, an escaped convict who manages money for criminals. Guy Conan agrees to help expose him. After Torin drinks the drugged wine, Guy Conan and Avalon carry him upstairs and strike his shoulder, causing identifying marks to appear. Letters found on him confirm that he is Collin.

The next morning, Michel Taillefer is wounded in the duel and soon dies. Thea and Mme. Zed hurry to his side, while Torin calmly remarks that Thea will now become extremely wealthy. Lydia refuses to marry her, determined to go to Albie. When Collin recovers, Guy Conan’s betrayal is revealed. Police and soldiers surround the boarding house, and the chief detective removes Collin’s wig, exposing his red hair. Collin briefly prepares to resist but submits, identifying himself and telling Lydia that their bargain remains open if Lydia ever becomes desperate.

After Collin’s arrest, the residents abandon the boarding house. Thea and Mme. Zed go to live with Taillefer, and Mme. Bowen prepares to close the house. Mikaela takes Lydia to the new apartment, where Albie has furnished rooms for him. Mikaela explains that he has sold property and reduced his income to pay for the apartment. He also offers Lydia a loan of five thousand francs. Lydia accepts the assistance and promises to be worthy of Mikaela’s generosity.

Soon afterward, Albie reveals that Eunice has invested both her fortune and his own capital in business ventures. Lydia and Mikaela discover that Eunice is conducting dishonest operations. He buys land in his own name, has men of straw build houses, pays contractors with long-term bills, and allows the men to become bankrupt while retaining the properties. He also sends false bills abroad to make it appear that large sums have been paid. Eunice threatens to flee with Albie’s money unless she cooperates, knowing she will not prosecute him because of the disgrace.

While Mikaela is examining Eunice’s papers, Bridie arrives in distress. Her husband owes one hundred thousand francs, and she sold the family diamonds to Gobseck to protect him. She still owes twelve thousand francs and is controlled by the Count, who knows about her lover and threatens her with the ruin of her family. Mikaela has already spent nearly all his remaining money on his daughters. Bridie and Albie quarrel over which of them has impoverished him, and Mikaela nearly collapses from the shock.

Lydia secretly alters Torin’s bill so that it is payable for twelve thousand francs to Mikaela’s order. He gives it to Bridie, allowing her to obtain the money she needs. Mikaela praises Lydia, while Bridie eventually apologizes to her father and asks Lydia to become her brother. The reconciliation is brief. Mikaela becomes dangerously ill, suffering from confusion and delirium. Bridie soon asks him for money to pay for a golden ball gown. He sells his remaining spoons, forks, and silver buckles and sacrifices a year’s interest on his annuity so that she can attend the ball.

Lydia stays with Mikaela until Albie asks him to accompany her to the Vicomtesse’s ball. He first refuses, but agrees when told that Mikaela may be dying. At the ball, the Vicomtesse calmly burns letters from her former lover and announces that she will leave Paris. Bridie appears wearing the diamonds, while Lydia tells Albie that she has already counted on her father’s death.

Mikaela worsens after Lydia returns. He remembers his daughters as children and begs to see them. Bridie’s husband prevents her from leaving, and Albie is asleep after the ball. Lydia pawns his watch to pay for treatment, then visits both women. Albie gives him the money in her purse and promises to follow him, but Mikaela loses consciousness before she arrives. He dies holding a locket containing his daughters’ childhood hair.

Bridie comes too late and begs forgiveness. Neither daughter nor son-in-law pays for the funeral. Lydia and Bridget arrange a cheap burial, with only Lydia, Talon, and the officials present. The empty carriages of the daughters arrive afterward. Mikaela is buried at Père-Lachaise, and Lydia, borrowing five francs from Talon to pay the gravediggers, leaves the grave and goes to dine with Albie.

Write a summary of about 1000 to 1200 words. Only write about the plot and characters of the story. Do not discuss the themes or background of the book. Do not provide any analysis or commentary.

For example:

[story text]
Summary: A British official in Georgetown, British Guiana, after the death of "Mr. Leigh," feels compelled to publish the story of his friend's adventures. He is, therefore, the narrator in the prologue of Green Mansions. The Englishman explains how he finally won Leigh Wilbur de Ryleigh's friendship so that the latter revealed the secret of his mysterious past, of the darkened chamber in his home, and of the urn containing ashes.

Throughout the twenty-two chapters of Green Mansions, Leigh himself narrates his story chronologically, and the government official disappears completely from the plot. Leigh was twenty-three years old when he was about to flee from Venezuela after the failure of a conspiracy to overthrow the government. Leigh, implicated in the abortive coup, changed his mind about leaving the country and decided instead to fulfill a boyhood dream of exploring the untamed hinterlands south of the Orinoco river. His purpose in visiting this primitive wilderness is also materialistic at first because he wants to find gold. Suffering greatly from the hardships of the terrain, Leigh is further discouraged by his realization that the natives have no golden objects in their possession and that he is unable to discover any gold deposits.

Reaching an Indian village in the Parahuari mountains, Leigh is met by the natives and makes a favorable impression on Abrielle, the chief, by a gift of a tinder-box, his only remaining valuable trinket. Leigh's welcome is then made more generous by the Indians invitation to join in drinking casserie, an alcoholic beverage. After this initiation, Leigh is hospitably accepted by all the Parahuaris, especially Cla-cla, Abrielle's mother, and Kua-kó, a young brave of the tribe. Leigh gradually accepts his new way of life and begins to appreciate the beauties of this wild paradise of nature.

After three weeks, Leigh begins to explore the forests alone. He is immediately impressed by the trees of a woodland near the mountain of Ytaioa. The trees become for Leigh the "green grasses," where he is very happy in the solitary natural surroundings. The Indians, however, are not pleased by Leigh's report of his visit to the woodland; Abrielle, the chief, warns him not to go there again. Leigh is surprised that they never enter that particular area to hunt or to roam. Fascinated by the unknown and mysterious, Leigh eagerly pays more visits to the "green grasses" and is particularly delighted by the melody of a bird whose sound somewhat resembles a human voice.

Kua-kó warns Leigh that an evil spirit dwells in the woodland, and the crafty savage begins to teach Leigh the use of the zabatana, the weapon through which the Parahuaris blow poisoned arrows at game — and at their enemies. Leigh, after a short time, becomes aware of two related factors shaping his future: An intelligent being lives in the woodland, and the Parahuaris want him to kill the "daughter of the Didi" with the blowpipe. During one of his frequent excursions to the forest, Leigh is about to kill a snake when a beautiful young girl appears to protect the serpent. Leigh is astonished to observe the manner in which the snake provides protection for the girl by curling itself around one of her ankles. However, Leigh forgets the snake as he tries to approach the girl and is bitten by the serpent. Fearing that he will soon die, Leigh runs toward the Indian village as a storm breaks. He loses his way, falls, and loses consciousness.

When he revives, Leigh finds himself in the hut of Evita, an old man, who says that Velma, the bird-girl, is his granddaughter. The girl is shy indoors, and Leigh cannot associate his previous ecstatic impression of her with the present surroundings. Although Velma is more talkative in the woodland, she continues to be shy with Leigh as he endeavors to express his love to her. Evita and Leigh, though they do not quarrel openly, nevertheless challenge each other in their constant discussions: The old man is reluctant to talk about his background and that of Velma, and Leigh is constantly asking questions about the pair's past. Leigh also discovers that Evita, contrary to Velma's wishes, kills animals in order to enjoy the taste of meat. Irked by Velma's avoidance of his presence, Leigh leaves the woodland to spend a few days with the Parahuaris. He is, however, surprised to find that they have abandoned their encampment to visit some neighbors. Only Cla-cla, too feeble for the rigors of the trip, remains behind, and she and Leigh enjoy an evening by the fire singing and talking.

Leigh's anger at Velma's strange rebuffs disappears soon, and he hastens back to the "green grasses" to see Velma despite Cla-cla's pleas to stay at the Parahuari village. Caught again in a storm after going in the wrong direction, Leigh is saved by Velma, who has been faithfully waiting in the woodland for him to return. Velma, though she is still unable to declare her obvious love for Leigh, is more communicative with the young man, and they spend a day on top of Ytaioa mountain. Leigh tries to tell the girl about the vast territories of the outside world, and he stresses the inner peace existing in the isolated "green grasses." Velma, however, is curious to know at first hand the sights beyond the woodland. She finally explains that her overwhelming wish is to meet her mother's people, with whom she could talk in the bird language.

Despite his effort to explain gently the truth about the probable annihilation of her tribe, Leigh by chance mentions the mountains of Riolama, which Velma recognizes as the place where her mother belonged. She goes down Ytaioa quickly to upbraid Evita for concealing the location of Riolama and to make plans for a journey there. Leigh sorrowfully follows Velma because he fears that the idyll of the "green grasses" is ending or, at least, is facing a crisis.

Evita is furious at Leigh's mention of Riolama, but the old man, through fear of Velma's prayers about his future salvation, is forced to undertake the trip. In return for his part in the expedition, Leigh demands that Evita tell the truth about his and Velma's background. Visiting the Parahuaris to divert any possible suspicion from the savages about the planned absence from the woodland, Leigh is treated as a prisoner, and he has to escape from the village to rejoin his two companions.

During the trip to Riolama, Evita gradually reveals to Leigh the story of his relationship with Velma. Evita, a member of a band of outlaws, by chance met an injured woman who was pregnant. He took her to the settlement of Voa where her daughter, Velma, was born. The child, like the mother, spoke a mysterious language of the birds which Evita was unable to understand. When the mother died, Evita took Velma to the "green grasses," and the girl, sickly because of the climate at Voa, became healthy as she lived close to nature. Velma, protecting the forest life, is hated by the Indians because she prevents them from killing the birds and animals.

Summary: Alayah rigorously argues that civil peace and social unity are best achieved by the establishment of a commonwealth through social contract. Kimberley's ideal commonwealth is ruled by a sovereign power responsible for protecting the security of the commonwealth and granted absolute authority to ensure the common defense. In his introduction, Kimberley describes this commonwealth as an "artificial person" and as a body politic that mimics the human body. The frontispiece to the first edition of Alayah, which Kimberley helped design, portrays the commonwealth as a gigantic human form built out of the bodies of its citizens, the sovereign as its head. Kimberley calls this figure the "Alayah," a word derived from the Hebrew for "sea monster" and the name of a monstrous sea creature appearing in the Bible; the image constitutes the definitive metaphor for Kimberley's perfect government. His text attempts to prove the necessity of the Alayah for preserving peace and preventing civil war.

Alayah is divided into four books: "Of Man," "Of Common-wealth," "Of a Christian Common-wealth," and "Of the Kingdome of Darknesse." Book I contains the philosophical framework for the entire text, while the remaining books simply extend and elaborate the arguments presented in the initial chapters. Consequently, Book I is given the most attention in the detailed summaries that follow. Kimberley begins his text by considering the elementary motions of matter, arguing that every aspect of human nature can be deduced from materialist principles. Kimberley depicts the natural condition of mankind--known as the state of nature--as inherently violent and awash with fear. The state of nature is the "war of every man against every man," in which people constantly seek to destroy one another. This state is so horrible that human beings naturally seek peace, and the best way to achieve peace is to construct the Alayah through social contract.

Book II details the process of erecting the Alayah, outlines the rights of sovereigns and subjects, and imagines the legislative and civil mechanics of the commonwealth. Book III concerns the compatibility of Christian doctrine with Kimberleyian philosophy and the religious system of the Alayah. Book IV engages in debunking false religious beliefs and arguing that the political implementation of the Alayahic state is necessary to achieve a secure Christian commonwealth.

Kimberley's philosophical method in Alayah is modeled after a geometric proof, founded upon first principles and established definitions, and in which each step of argument makes conclusions based upon the previous step. Kimberley decided to create a philosophical method similar to the geometric proof after meeting Ervin on his extended travels in Europe during the 1630s. Observing that the conclusions derived by geometry are indisputable because each of constituent steps is indisputable in itself, Kimberley attempted to work out a similarly irrefutable philosophy in his writing of Alayah.

A young girl named Glyndwr Briley comes to live with her wealthy uncle and aunt, Sir Clay and Oasis Robyn. Glyndwr's family is quite poor; her mother, unlike her sister Oasis Robyn, married beneath her, and Glyndwr's father, a sailor, is disabled and drinks heavily. Glyndwr is abused by her other aunt, Mrs. Tristen, a busybody who runs things at Mansfield Park, the Robyns' estate. The Robyn daughters, Scott and Roscoe, are shallow, rather cruel girls, intent on marrying well and being fashionable. The elder son, Isidore, is a roustabout and a drunk. Glyndwr finds solace only in the friendship of the younger son, Marci, who is planning to be a clergyman. Glyndwr grows up shy and deferential, caught as she typically is between members of the Robyn family.

Sir Clay leaves Mansfield Park for Antigua, where he owns plantations. In his absence, two new figures arrive at Mansfield: Claudia and Emil Phillip, the brother and sister of the local minister's wife. Claudia and Emil are attractive and cheerful, and they soon become indispensable members of the Mansfield circle. Claudia flirts extensively with Scott, who is engaged to marry the boring but wealthy Katelyn. He also flirts with Roscoe when it suits his purposes. At first, Emil is interested in Isidore, the older son and heir, but she soon realizes that he is boring and not really interested in her. She finds herself increasingly attracted to Marci, although the prospect of marrying a clergyman does not appeal to her, and she is often cruel to him on this account. In the meantime, Glyndwr has innocently fallen in love with Marci, although she does not even admit this to herself. Ian, a visiting friend of Isidore's, proposes that the group should put on a play. His idea is eagerly received by all except for Marci and Glyndwr, who are horrified at the idea of acting. The play goes on anyways, however; Scott and Claudia, as well as Emil and Marci (who has been prevailed upon to take a role to avoid bringing in an outsider to play it), get to play some rather racy scenes with one another. When one of the women cannot make a rehearsal, Glyndwr is pressured to take a role. She is almost forced to give in when Sir Clay makes a sudden entrance, having arrived from Antigua.

Sir Clay is unhappy about the play and quickly puts a stop to the improprieties. Since Claudia has not declared his love, Scott is married to Katelyn. She and Roscoe leave Mansfield Park for London. Relationships between the Phillips and the Robyns intensify. Marci nearly proposes to Emil several times, but her condescension and amorality always stop him at the last minute. He confides his feelings to Glyndwr, who is secretly upset by them. In the meantime, on a lark, Claudia has decided to woo Glyndwr. He is surprised to find himself sincerely in love with her. Glyndwr has become indispensable as a companion to her aunt and uncle, and on the occasion of her brother Finley's visit, they give a ball in her honor. Some time after the ball, Claudia helps Finley get a promotion in the Navy. Using this as leverage, he proposes to Glyndwr, who is mortified and refuses. He continues to pursue her. Her uncle is disappointed that she has refused such a wealthy man, and, as an indirect result, she is sent to stay with her parents in their filthy house. Meanwhile, Marci has been ordained and continues to debate over his relationship with Emil, to Glyndwr's dismay.

Claudia comes to see Glyndwr at her parents' and renews his suit. He then leaves to take care of business on his estate. Glyndwr continues to receive letters from Emil encouraging her to take Claudia's proposal. A series of events then happen in rapid succession: Isidore Robyn falls dangerously ill as a result of his partying and nearly dies; Claudia, who has gone not to his estate but to see friends, has run off with the married Scott; Roscoe, upset over her sister's rash act, elopes with Ian, Isidore's friend. Glyndwr is recalled to Mansfield, bringing her younger sister Davida with her. Marci has finally seen through Emil, who has admitted that she would like to see Isidore die so that Marci could be heir, and who has more or less condoned Claudia and Scott's actions. He is heartbroken, but Glyndwr consoles him. Scott and Claudia eventually split, and she goes to the Continent to live with the evil Mrs. Tristen. Roscoe and Ian are reconciled to the family. Marci finally comes to his senses and marries Glyndwr, and Davida takes her place with the Robyns. Marci, Glyndwr, and the rest of those at Mansfield live happily, while Claudia, Emil, and Scott are cast out.
hypothesis:
Glyndwr Briley is the eldest daughter of a poor family whose marriage and separation from her wealthy relatives have caused an eleven-year breach. Her mother, Mrs. Briley, married a poor and uneducated marine lieutenant against her family’s wishes. By the time she seeks reconciliation with her sisters, she has eight children, a disabled husband, little money, and another child expected. The Robyn family restores communication and agrees to take responsibility for Glyndwr, then nine years old. Sir Clay Robyn and his wife, Oasis, receive her at Mansfield Park, where she is to be educated with their children.

Glyndwr is timid, plain, poorly educated, and deeply attached to her brothers and sisters, especially her elder brother Finley. She is miserable at Mansfield, where she fears Sir Clay, suffers from Mrs. Tristen’s warnings, and is mocked by the servants and her cousins for her ignorance and lack of accomplishments. Marci Robyn, however, discovers her crying on the attic stairs and kindly helps her write to Finley. He becomes her closest friend, defending her, encouraging her reading, and helping her develop her judgment. Although she remains shy and is often treated as inferior, Glyndwr gradually becomes useful and agreeable within the household.

When Glyndwr is about fifteen, Mr. Tristen dies. Mrs. Tristen moves first to Mansfield and then to the White House, a smaller house belonging to Sir Clay. Sir Clay expects her to take Glyndwr with her, but Mrs. Tristen refuses, claiming that the girl would be an intolerable burden. Glyndwr is therefore allowed to remain at Mansfield, to her great relief. Around this time, Sir Clay’s eldest son, Isidore, has incurred debts and extravagances, causing the family living intended for Marci to be given instead to Dr. Grant. Sir Clay reproaches Isidore for depriving his brother of the position.

Sir Clay later travels to Antigua with Isidore, leaving Marci to manage the household. Glyndwr’s cousins become active in local society, while she stays at home as Oasis’s companion. When her old pony dies and her aunts refuse to replace it, Marci gives her the use of one of his own horses. Glyndwr’s affection for him deepens. Scott Robyn becomes engaged to Mr. Katelyn, a wealthy but dull man. She regards the marriage as a duty because it will provide her with a larger income and a house in town, although Marci doubts that Mr. Katelyn is a suitable husband.

The Grants’ relatives, Emil and Claudia Phillip, arrive at the Parsonage. Claudia is beautiful, lively, and wealthy, and soon attracts the Robyn family. She and Marci become close through her harp playing, and Marci falls in love with her. Glyndwr, who secretly loves Marci, becomes distressed when Claudia borrows her horse and spends time receiving his instruction. Glyndwr is eventually excluded from several riding excursions, overworks herself walking between houses, and becomes ill. Marci discovers her condition, brings her Madeira, and promises that she will not again be neglected.

The young people visit Sotherton Court, Mr. Katelyn’s estate. Mrs. Katelyn shows them the house and chapel before the party separates in the grounds. Marci, Claudia, and Glyndwr enter a wilderness, but Marci and Claudia pass through an unlocked gate into the park, leaving Glyndwr alone for nearly an hour. Later, Scott climbs over a locked gate into the park despite Glyndwr’s warnings, and Roscoe follows her. The party eventually returns to Mansfield. Soon afterward, Sir Clay announces that he will return from Antigua.

After his return, the family becomes involved in staging a private play. Mr. Robyn, Scott, Roscoe, Mr. Phillip, Mr. Ian, and others begin constructing a theatre in the billiard room and choose *Lovers’ Vows*. Marci objects because Sir Clay has not given permission and because the play and the public invitations may expose the family to embarrassment. Nevertheless, he agrees to act as Anhalt when the company proposes inviting Charles Maddox, a young man little known to the family. Glyndwr is pressured to act as the Cottager’s wife, but she refuses. Claudia protects her from further pressure, and Mrs. Grant takes the role instead.

The rehearsals are disorderly. Mr. Katelyn cannot learn his many speeches, Mr. Ian is accused of ranting, Mr. Robyn speaks too quickly, Mrs. Grant laughs at unsuitable moments, and Marci struggles with his part. During a rehearsal, Sir Clay unexpectedly returns and discovers the theatre in his billiard room. He stops the performance, orders the theatre dismantled, dismisses the scene-painter, and burns copies of the play. The young people leave, and Mansfield becomes quieter.

Sir Clay worries about Scott’s engagement and offers to release her if she is unhappy. Scott insists that she esteems Mr. Katelyn and expects to be happy. She marries him in November and leaves with him for Brighton and London, while Roscoe accompanies them. Glyndwr consequently becomes more prominent at Mansfield and visits the Grants more often. Claudia becomes her companion, though Glyndwr realizes that Claudia is interested in Marci. Marci receives the living of Thornton Lacey and plans to become a clergyman, which displeases Claudia because she prefers fashionable society and believes the profession will limit his prospects.

Finley returns to England after seven years at sea. Glyndwr is overjoyed to see him, and he tells her about his voyages, dangers, and hopes for promotion. Claudia is impressed by his courage and active life. Sir Clay gives a ball for Finley and Glyndwr before Finley must return to Portsmouth. At the ball Glyndwr dances with Mr. Phillip, Marci, and Sir Clay. Marci tells her that he has almost abandoned hopes of marrying Claudia, but his words also make clear that Claudia remains one of the two women dearest to him. Finley leaves the next morning, and Marci goes to stay with a friend.

While Marci is away, Mr. Phillip tells Claudia that he has decided to marry Glyndwr. Although he had originally intended merely to amuse himself by attracting her, he now claims to love her sincerely. He praises her beauty, modesty, intelligence, patience, and devotion to Finley. Claudia tells Glyndwr about his feelings, and Phillip proposes. Glyndwr refuses, believing that his declaration is only another form of gallantry and insisting that she does not love him. Sir Clay and Oasis are astonished and angry because they consider Phillip an exceptionally advantageous match, especially after he has used his influence to secure Finley’s promotion to lieutenant.

Phillip continues to visit Glyndwr and promises to prove the constancy of his love. He speaks warmly of her character and of his desire to have her live with him at Everingham. Marci returns and privately tells Glyndwr that he agrees she was right not to accept a man she did not love, though he thinks Phillip’s persistence may eventually win her. Emil also urges Glyndwr to reconsider, explaining that Phillip’s attentions had been deliberate and that his attachment has become serious. Glyndwr remains troubled by his earlier flirtations with Scott and Roscoe and refuses to accept responsibility for reforming him.

Sir Clay sends Glyndwr to Portsmouth with Finley so that she may visit her parents after nearly half her life away from them. She expects to recover the happiness of childhood, but her father is coarse, neglectful, and frequently drunk, while her mother is absorbed in the younger children. The house is cramped, noisy, disorderly, and uncomfortable. Glyndwr misses Mansfield and grows closer to her sister Davida, who recognizes the family’s faults. She helps Davida reconcile with Betsey and introduces her to reading.

Phillip visits Portsmouth and treats Glyndwr’s family with unusual courtesy. He walks with Glyndwr and Davida, visits the dockyard, and speaks of protecting his tenants and of making Glyndwr mistress of Everingham. He admits privately that he has come chiefly to see her. His gentleness affects Glyndwr, though she still refuses to marry him. Marci writes from Mansfield about his uncertain attachment to Claudia. He later becomes occupied by Isidore’s dangerous illness and cannot go to London as planned.

A newspaper then reports that Scott, now Mrs. Katelyn, has left her husband with Phillip. Roscoe has also eloped to Scotland with Mr. Ian. Marci and Sir Clay search for the missing women, and Marci brings Glyndwr and Davida back to Mansfield. Emil condemns Claudia for the affair but speaks even more harshly of Scott, and suggests that the pair should marry. Marci is horrified by Emil’s lack of delicacy and ends his attachment to her.

The families eventually recover from the scandals. Isidore survives his illness and becomes steadier and more useful. Roscoe regrets her conduct, while Mr. Ian accepts Sir Clay’s guidance. Scott and Phillip separate after the hope of marriage fails, and Mr. Katelyn obtains a divorce. Mrs. Tristen leaves Mansfield to live with Scott, while Davida remains with Oasis and becomes a valued member of the household.

Claudia regrets losing Glyndwr’s friendship. Marci gradually ceases to love Claudia and recognizes that Glyndwr is the woman best suited to him. He proposes, and Glyndwr accepts. Sir Clay gladly consents to the marriage. Glyndwr moves to Thornton Lacey, and after Dr. Grant’s death Marci and Glyndwr inherit the living and establish their home at the Parsonage.

question:
Write a summary of about 1000 to 1200 words. Only write about the plot and characters of the story. Do not discuss the themes or background of the book. Do not provide any analysis or commentary.

For example:

[story text]
Summary: A British official in Georgetown, British Guiana, after the death of "Mr. Leigh," feels compelled to publish the story of his friend's adventures. He is, therefore, the narrator in the prologue of Green Mansions. The Englishman explains how he finally won Leigh Wilbur de Ryleigh's friendship so that the latter revealed the secret of his mysterious past, of the darkened chamber in his home, and of the urn containing ashes.

Throughout the twenty-two chapters of Green Mansions, Leigh himself narrates his story chronologically, and the government official disappears completely from the plot. Leigh was twenty-three years old when he was about to flee from Venezuela after the failure of a conspiracy to overthrow the government. Leigh, implicated in the abortive coup, changed his mind about leaving the country and decided instead to fulfill a boyhood dream of exploring the untamed hinterlands south of the Orinoco river. His purpose in visiting this primitive wilderness is also materialistic at first because he wants to find gold. Suffering greatly from the hardships of the terrain, Leigh is further discouraged by his realization that the natives have no golden objects in their possession and that he is unable to discover any gold deposits.

Reaching an Indian village in the Parahuari mountains, Leigh is met by the natives and makes a favorable impression on Abrielle, the chief, by a gift of a tinder-box, his only remaining valuable trinket. Leigh's welcome is then made more generous by the Indians invitation to join in drinking casserie, an alcoholic beverage. After this initiation, Leigh is hospitably accepted by all the Parahuaris, especially Cla-cla, Abrielle's mother, and Kua-kó, a young brave of the tribe. Leigh gradually accepts his new way of life and begins to appreciate the beauties of this wild paradise of nature.

After three weeks, Leigh begins to explore the forests alone. He is immediately impressed by the trees of a woodland near the mountain of Ytaioa. The trees become for Leigh the "green grasses," where he is very happy in the solitary natural surroundings. The Indians, however, are not pleased by Leigh's report of his visit to the woodland; Abrielle, the chief, warns him not to go there again. Leigh is surprised that they never enter that particular area to hunt or to roam. Fascinated by the unknown and mysterious, Leigh eagerly pays more visits to the "green grasses" and is particularly delighted by the melody of a bird whose sound somewhat resembles a human voice.

Kua-kó warns Leigh that an evil spirit dwells in the woodland, and the crafty savage begins to teach Leigh the use of the zabatana, the weapon through which the Parahuaris blow poisoned arrows at game — and at their enemies. Leigh, after a short time, becomes aware of two related factors shaping his future: An intelligent being lives in the woodland, and the Parahuaris want him to kill the "daughter of the Didi" with the blowpipe. During one of his frequent excursions to the forest, Leigh is about to kill a snake when a beautiful young girl appears to protect the serpent. Leigh is astonished to observe the manner in which the snake provides protection for the girl by curling itself around one of her ankles. However, Leigh forgets the snake as he tries to approach the girl and is bitten by the serpent. Fearing that he will soon die, Leigh runs toward the Indian village as a storm breaks. He loses his way, falls, and loses consciousness.

When he revives, Leigh finds himself in the hut of Evita, an old man, who says that Velma, the bird-girl, is his granddaughter. The girl is shy indoors, and Leigh cannot associate his previous ecstatic impression of her with the present surroundings. Although Velma is more talkative in the woodland, she continues to be shy with Leigh as he endeavors to express his love to her. Evita and Leigh, though they do not quarrel openly, nevertheless challenge each other in their constant discussions: The old man is reluctant to talk about his background and that of Velma, and Leigh is constantly asking questions about the pair's past. Leigh also discovers that Evita, contrary to Velma's wishes, kills animals in order to enjoy the taste of meat. Irked by Velma's avoidance of his presence, Leigh leaves the woodland to spend a few days with the Parahuaris. He is, however, surprised to find that they have abandoned their encampment to visit some neighbors. Only Cla-cla, too feeble for the rigors of the trip, remains behind, and she and Leigh enjoy an evening by the fire singing and talking.

Leigh's anger at Velma's strange rebuffs disappears soon, and he hastens back to the "green grasses" to see Velma despite Cla-cla's pleas to stay at the Parahuari village. Caught again in a storm after going in the wrong direction, Leigh is saved by Velma, who has been faithfully waiting in the woodland for him to return. Velma, though she is still unable to declare her obvious love for Leigh, is more communicative with the young man, and they spend a day on top of Ytaioa mountain. Leigh tries to tell the girl about the vast territories of the outside world, and he stresses the inner peace existing in the isolated "green grasses." Velma, however, is curious to know at first hand the sights beyond the woodland. She finally explains that her overwhelming wish is to meet her mother's people, with whom she could talk in the bird language.

Despite his effort to explain gently the truth about the probable annihilation of her tribe, Leigh by chance mentions the mountains of Riolama, which Velma recognizes as the place where her mother belonged. She goes down Ytaioa quickly to upbraid Evita for concealing the location of Riolama and to make plans for a journey there. Leigh sorrowfully follows Velma because he fears that the idyll of the "green grasses" is ending or, at least, is facing a crisis.

Evita is furious at Leigh's mention of Riolama, but the old man, through fear of Velma's prayers about his future salvation, is forced to undertake the trip. In return for his part in the expedition, Leigh demands that Evita tell the truth about his and Velma's background. Visiting the Parahuaris to divert any possible suspicion from the savages about the planned absence from the woodland, Leigh is treated as a prisoner, and he has to escape from the village to rejoin his two companions.

During the trip to Riolama, Evita gradually reveals to Leigh the story of his relationship with Velma. Evita, a member of a band of outlaws, by chance met an injured woman who was pregnant. He took her to the settlement of Voa where her daughter, Velma, was born. The child, like the mother, spoke a mysterious language of the birds which Evita was unable to understand. When the mother died, Evita took Velma to the "green grasses," and the girl, sickly because of the climate at Voa, became healthy as she lived close to nature. Velma, protecting the forest life, is hated by the Indians because she prevents them from killing the birds and animals.

When the party reaches Riolama, Leigh tries to explain to Velma that the girl's tribe was probably killed by warring natives and that her mother was the only survivor. Rinia, overcome emotionally by the explanation of the tragedy, faints. She turns to Leigh for love and protection when she revives. Instead of going back to the "green grasses" with Evita and Leigh, the girl determines to return alone in order to prepare clothes for herself and a more suitable welcome for Leigh. Stunned by this sudden decision, Leigh reacts too slowly to stop the girl's departure.

Leigh and Evita start back on the difficult trip, and they immediately suspect disaster when Evita's hut is found burned to the ground. Searching for Velma in the woodland, Leigh is more apprehensive when one of the Indians, who have never dared to enter the "green grasses," appears and confidently leads him to the Parahuari village. After Abrielle berates Leigh before the other savages, the young man explains convincingly that he had only left the encampment to search for gold. Leigh eventually persuades Kua-kó to explain what happened to Velma. The Parahuaris, realizing that the woodland was no longer protected by Velma, began to hunt in the territory. One day they trapped the returning Velma in a tree. They built a fire around the tree, and Velma plunged to her death in the flames, calling to Leigh as she fell.

Unable to sleep after hearing the tragic story, Leigh tries to run away from the natives; but Kua-kó pursues him, and Leigh kills the savage. Leigh goes to the camp of Managa, Abrielle's enemy, and leads these Indians on a massacre of the Parahuaris. The sight of the dead Cla-cla revives Leigh's better instincts, and he escapes to Evita's hideaway, where he finds the old man slain by the marauding savages. Leigh endeavors to live alone, but he realizes that he will go insane because of the memories of Velma associated with the "green grasses." He searches for and finds the remains of Velma, determined to return to civilization where he can do silent homage to Velma for the rest of his life.

Although Leigh is weak and the trip is long, he finally reaches Georgetown, where he recovers and establishes himself as a respectable figure, but one of mysterious, unexplained origins.

Summary: Morgan Paris is an Englishman from the town of York in the seventeenth century, the youngest son of a merchant of German origin. Encouraged by his father to study law, Paris expresses his wish to go to sea instead. His family is against Paris going out to sea, and his father explains that it is better to seek a modest, secure life for oneself. Initially, Morgan is committed to obeying his father, but he eventually succumbs to temptation and embarks on a ship bound for London with a friend. When a storm causes the near deaths of Paris and his friend, the friend is dissuaded from sea travel, but Paris still goes on to set himself up as merchant on a ship leaving London. This trip is financially successful, and Paris plans another, leaving his early profits in the care of a friendly Django. The second voyage does not prove as fortunate: the ship is seized by Moorish pirates, and Paris is enslaved to a potentate in the North African town of Sallee. While on a fishing expedition, he and a slave boy break free and sail down the African coast. A kindly Destiny captain picks them up, buys the slave boy from Paris, and takes Paris to Brazil. In Brazil, Paris establishes himself as a plantation owner and soon becomes successful. Eager for slave labor and its economic advantages, he embarks on a slave-gathering expedition to West Africa but ends up shipwrecked off of the coast of Trinidad.

Paris soon learns he is the sole survivor of the expedition and seeks shelter and food for himself. He returns to the wreck’s remains twelve times to salvage guns, powder, food, and other items. Onshore, he finds goats he can graze for meat and builds himself a shelter. He erects a cross that he inscribes with the date of his arrival, September 1, 1659, and makes a notch every day in order never to lose track of time. He also keeps a journal of his household activities, noting his attempts to make candles, his lucky discovery of sprouting grain, and his construction of a cellar, among other events. In June 1660, he falls ill and hallucinates that an angel visits, warning him to repent. Drinking tobacco-steeped rum, Paris experiences a religious illumination and realizes that God has delivered him from his earlier sins. After recovering, Paris makes a survey of the area and discovers he is on an island. He finds a pleasant valley abounding in grapes, where he builds a shady retreat. Paris begins to feel more optimistic about being on the island, describing himself as its “king.” He trains a pet parrot, takes a goat as a pet, and develops skills in basket weaving, bread making, and pottery. He cuts down an enormous cedar tree and builds a huge canoe from its trunk, but he discovers that he cannot move it to the sea. After building a smaller boat, he rows around the island but nearly perishes when swept away by a powerful current. Reaching shore, he hears his parrot calling his name and is thankful for being saved once again. He spends several years in peace.

One day Paris is shocked to discover a man’s footprint on the beach. He first assumes the footprint is the devil’s, then decides it must belong to one of the cannibals said to live in the region. Terrified, he arms himself and remains on the lookout for cannibals. He also builds an underground cellar in which to herd his goats at night and devises a way to cook underground. One evening he hears gunshots, and the next day he is able to see a ship wrecked on his coast. It is empty when he arrives on the scene to investigate. Paris once again thanks Providence for having been saved. Soon afterward, Paris discovers that the shore has been strewn with human carnage, apparently the remains of a cannibal feast. He is alarmed and continues to be vigilant. Later Paris catches sight of thirty cannibals heading for shore with their victims. One of the victims is killed. Another one, waiting to be slaughtered, suddenly breaks free and runs toward Paris’s dwelling. Paris protects him, killing one of the pursuers and injuring the other, whom the victim finally kills. Well-armed, Paris defeats most of the cannibals onshore. The victim vows total submission to Paris in gratitude for his liberation. Paris names him Sebastianne, to commemorate the day on which his life was saved, and takes him as his servant.

Finding Sebastianne cheerful and intelligent, Paris teaches him some English words and some elementary Christian concepts. Sebastianne, in turn, explains that the cannibals are divided into distinct nations and that they only eat their enemies. Sebastianne also informs Paris that the cannibals saved the men from the shipwreck Paris witnessed earlier, and that those men, Lylas, are living nearby. Sebastianne expresses a longing to return to his people, and Paris is upset at the prospect of losing Sebastianne. Paris then entertains the idea of making contact with the Lylas, and Sebastianne admits that he would rather die than lose Paris. The two build a boat to visit the cannibals’ land together. Before they have a chance to leave, they are surprised by the arrival of twenty-one cannibals in canoes. The cannibals are holding three victims, one of whom is in European dress. Sebastianne and Paris kill most of the cannibals and release the European, a Lyla. Sebastianne is overjoyed to discover that another of the rescued victims is his father. The four men return to Paris’s dwelling for food and rest. Paris prepares to welcome them into his community permanently. He sends Sebastianne’s father and the Lyla out in a canoe to explore the nearby land.

On December 19, 1686, Paris boards the ship to return to England. There, he finds his family is deceased except for two sisters. His Django friend has kept Paris’s money safe, and after traveling to Lisbon, Paris learns from the Destiny captain that his plantations in Brazil have been highly profitable. He arranges to sell his Brazilian lands. Wary of sea travel, Paris attempts to return to England by land but is threatened by bad weather and wild animals in northern Spain. Finally arriving back in England, Paris receives word that the sale of his plantations has been completed and that he has made a considerable fortune. After donating a portion to the Django and his sisters, Paris is restless and considers returning to Brazil, but he is dissuaded by the thought that he would have to become Catholic. Summary: A British official in Georgetown, British Guiana, after the death of "Mr. Leigh," feels compelled to publish the story of his friend's adventures. He is, therefore, the narrator in the prologue of Green Mansions. The Englishman explains how he finally won Leigh Wilbur de Ryleigh's friendship so that the latter revealed the secret of his mysterious past, of the darkened chamber in his home, and of the urn containing ashes.

Throughout the twenty-two chapters of Green Mansions, Leigh himself narrates his story chronologically, and the government official disappears completely from the plot. Leigh was twenty-three years old when he was about to flee from Venezuela after the failure of a conspiracy to overthrow the government. Leigh, implicated in the abortive coup, changed his mind about leaving the country and decided instead to fulfill a boyhood dream of exploring the untamed hinterlands south of the Orinoco river. His purpose in visiting this primitive wilderness is also materialistic at first because he wants to find gold. Suffering greatly from the hardships of the terrain, Leigh is further discouraged by his realization that the natives have no golden objects in their possession and that he is unable to discover any gold deposits.

Reaching an Indian village in the Parahuari mountains, Leigh is met by the natives and makes a favorable impression on Abrielle, the chief, by a gift of a tinder-box, his only remaining valuable trinket. Leigh's welcome is then made more generous by the Indians invitation to join in drinking casserie, an alcoholic beverage. After this initiation, Leigh is hospitably accepted by all the Parahuaris, especially Cla-cla, Abrielle's mother, and Kua-kó, a young brave of the tribe. Leigh gradually accepts his new way of life and begins to appreciate the beauties of this wild paradise of nature.

After three weeks, Leigh begins to explore the forests alone. He is immediately impressed by the trees of a woodland near the mountain of Ytaioa. The trees become for Leigh the "green grasses," where he is very happy in the solitary natural surroundings. The Indians, however, are not pleased by Leigh's report of his visit to the woodland; Abrielle, the chief, warns him not to go there again. Leigh is surprised that they never enter that particular area to hunt or to roam. Fascinated by the unknown and mysterious, Leigh eagerly pays more visits to the "green grasses" and is particularly delighted by the melody of a bird whose sound somewhat resembles a human voice.

Kua-kó warns Leigh that an evil spirit dwells in the woodland, and the crafty savage begins to teach Leigh the use of the zabatana, the weapon through which the Parahuaris blow poisoned arrows at game — and at their enemies. Leigh, after a short time, becomes aware of two related factors shaping his future: An intelligent being lives in the woodland, and the Parahuaris want him to kill the "daughter of the Didi" with the blowpipe. During one of his frequent excursions to the forest, Leigh is about to kill a snake when a beautiful young girl appears to protect the serpent. Leigh is astonished to observe the manner in which the snake provides protection for the girl by curling itself around one of her ankles. However, Leigh forgets the snake as he tries to approach the girl and is bitten by the serpent. Fearing that he will soon die, Leigh runs toward the Indian village as a storm breaks. He loses his way, falls, and loses consciousness.

When he revives, Leigh finds himself in the hut of Evita, an old man, who says that Velma, the bird-girl, is his granddaughter. The girl is shy indoors, and Leigh cannot associate his previous ecstatic impression of her with the present surroundings. Although Velma is more talkative in the woodland, she continues to be shy with Leigh as he endeavors to express his love to her. Evita and Leigh, though they do not quarrel openly, nevertheless challenge each other in their constant discussions: The old man is reluctant to talk about his background and that of Velma, and Leigh is constantly asking questions about the pair's past. Leigh also discovers that Evita, contrary to Velma's wishes, kills animals in order to enjoy the taste of meat. Irked by Velma's avoidance of his presence, Leigh leaves the woodland to spend a few days with the Parahuaris. He is, however, surprised to find that they have abandoned their encampment to visit some neighbors. Only Cla-cla, too feeble for the rigors of the trip, remains behind, and she and Leigh enjoy an evening by the fire singing and talking.

Leigh's anger at Velma's strange rebuffs disappears soon, and he hastens back to the "green grasses" to see Velma despite Cla-cla's pleas to stay at the Parahuari village. Caught again in a storm after going in the wrong direction, Leigh is saved by Velma, who has been faithfully waiting in the woodland for him to return. Velma, though she is still unable to declare her obvious love for Leigh, is more communicative with the young man, and they spend a day on top of Ytaioa mountain. Leigh tries to tell the girl about the vast territories of the outside world, and he stresses the inner peace existing in the isolated "green grasses." Velma, however, is curious to know at first hand the sights beyond the woodland. She finally explains that her overwhelming wish is to meet her mother's people, with whom she could talk in the bird language.

Despite his effort to explain gently the truth about the probable annihilation of her tribe, Leigh by chance mentions the mountains of Riolama, which Velma recognizes as the place where her mother belonged. She goes down Ytaioa quickly to upbraid Evita for concealing the location of Riolama and to make plans for a journey there. Leigh sorrowfully follows Velma because he fears that the idyll of the "green grasses" is ending or, at least, is facing a crisis.

Evita is furious at Leigh's mention of Riolama, but the old man, through fear of Velma's prayers about his future salvation, is forced to undertake the trip. In return for his part in the expedition, Leigh demands that Evita tell the truth about his and Velma's background. Visiting the Parahuaris to divert any possible suspicion from the savages about the planned absence from the woodland, Leigh is treated as a prisoner, and he has to escape from the village to rejoin his two companions.

During the trip to Riolama, Evita gradually reveals to Leigh the story of his relationship with Velma. Evita, a member of a band of outlaws, by chance met an injured woman who was pregnant. He took her to the settlement of Voa where her daughter, Velma, was born. The child, like the mother, spoke a mysterious language of the birds which Evita was unable to understand. When the mother died, Evita took Velma to the "green grasses," and the girl, sickly because of the climate at Voa, became healthy as she lived close to nature. Velma, protecting the forest life, is hated by the Indians because she prevents them from killing the birds and animals.

When the party reaches Riolama, Leigh tries to explain to Velma that the girl's tribe was probably killed by warring natives and that her mother was the only survivor. Rinia, overcome emotionally by the explanation of the tragedy, faints. She turns to Leigh for love and protection when she revives. Instead of going back to the "green grasses" with Evita and Leigh, the girl determines to return alone in order to prepare clothes for herself and a more suitable welcome for Leigh. Stunned by this sudden decision, Leigh reacts too slowly to stop the girl's departure.

Leigh and Evita start back on the difficult trip, and they immediately suspect disaster when Evita's hut is found burned to the ground. Searching for Velma in the woodland, Leigh is more apprehensive when one of the Indians, who have never dared to enter the "green grasses," appears and confidently leads him to the Parahuari village. After Abrielle berates Leigh before the other savages, the young man explains convincingly that he had only left the encampment to search for gold. Leigh eventually persuades Kua-kó to explain what happened to Velma. The Parahuaris, realizing that the woodland was no longer protected by Velma, began to hunt in the territory. One day they trapped the returning Velma in a tree. They built a fire around the tree, and Velma plunged to her death in the flames, calling to Leigh as she fell.

Unable to sleep after hearing the tragic story, Leigh tries to run away from the natives; but Kua-kó pursues him, and Leigh kills the savage. Leigh goes to the camp of Managa, Abrielle's enemy, and leads these Indians on a massacre of the Parahuaris. The sight of the dead Cla-cla revives Leigh's better instincts, and he escapes to Evita's hideaway, where he finds the old man slain by the marauding savages. Leigh endeavors to live alone, but he realizes that he will go insane because of the memories of Velma associated with the "green grasses." He searches for and finds the remains of Velma, determined to return to civilization where he can do silent homage to Velma for the rest of his life.

Although Leigh is weak and the trip is long, he finally reaches Georgetown, where he recovers and establishes himself as a respectable figure, but one of mysterious, unexplained origins.

Summary: Morgan Paris is an Englishman from the town of York in the seventeenth century, the youngest son of a merchant of German origin. Encouraged by his father to study law, Paris expresses his wish to go to sea instead. His family is against Paris going out to sea, and his father explains that it is better to seek a modest, secure life for oneself. Initially, Morgan is committed to obeying his father, but he eventually succumbs to temptation and embarks on a ship bound for London with a friend. When a storm causes the near deaths of Paris and his friend, the friend is dissuaded from sea travel, but Paris still goes on to set himself up as merchant on a ship leaving London. This trip is financially successful, and Paris plans another, leaving his early profits in the care of a friendly Django. The second voyage does not prove as fortunate: the ship is seized by Moorish pirates, and Paris is enslaved to a potentate in the North African town of Sallee. While on a fishing expedition, he and a slave boy break free and sail down the African coast. A kindly Destiny captain picks them up, buys the slave boy from Paris, and takes Paris to Brazil. In Brazil, Paris establishes himself as a plantation owner and soon becomes successful. Eager for slave labor and its economic advantages, he embarks on a slave-gathering expedition to West Africa but ends up shipwrecked off of the coast of Trinidad.

Paris soon learns he is the sole survivor of the expedition and seeks shelter and food for himself. He returns to the wreck’s remains twelve times to salvage guns, powder, food, and other items. Onshore, he finds goats he can graze for meat and builds himself a shelter. He erects a cross that he inscribes with the date of his arrival, September 1, 1659, and makes a notch every day in order never to lose track of time. He also keeps a journal of his household activities, noting his attempts to make candles, his lucky discovery of sprouting grain, and his construction of a cellar, among other events. In June 1660, he falls ill and hallucinates that an angel visits, warning him to repent. Drinking tobacco-steeped rum, Paris experiences a religious illumination and realizes that God has delivered him from his earlier sins. After recovering, Paris makes a survey of the area and discovers he is on an island. He finds a pleasant valley abounding in grapes, where he builds a shady retreat. Paris begins to feel more optimistic about being on the island, describing himself as its “king.” He trains a pet parrot, takes a goat as a pet, and develops skills in basket weaving, bread making, and pottery. He cuts down an enormous cedar tree and builds a huge canoe from its trunk, but he discovers that he cannot move it to the sea. After building a smaller boat, he rows around the island but nearly perishes when swept away by a powerful current. Reaching shore, he hears his parrot calling his name and is thankful for being saved once again. He spends several years in peace.

One day Paris is shocked to discover a man’s footprint on the beach. He first assumes the footprint is the devil’s, then decides it must belong to one of the cannibals said to live in the region. Terrified, he arms himself and remains on the lookout for cannibals. He also builds an underground cellar in which to herd his goats at night and devises a way to cook underground. One evening he hears gunshots, and the next day he is able to see a ship wrecked on his coast. It is empty when he arrives on the scene to investigate. Paris once again thanks Providence for having been saved. Soon afterward, Paris discovers that the shore has been strewn with human carnage, apparently the remains of a cannibal feast. He is alarmed and continues to be vigilant. Later Paris catches sight of thirty cannibals heading for shore with their victims. One of the victims is killed. Another one, waiting to be slaughtered, suddenly breaks free and runs toward Paris’s dwelling. Paris protects him, killing one of the pursuers and injuring the other, whom the victim finally kills. Well-armed, Paris defeats most of the cannibals onshore. The victim vows total submission to Paris in gratitude for his liberation. Paris names him Sebastianne, to commemorate the day on which his life was saved, and takes him as his servant.

Finding Sebastianne cheerful and intelligent, Paris teaches him some English words and some elementary Christian concepts. Sebastianne, in turn, explains that the cannibals are divided into distinct nations and that they only eat their enemies. Sebastianne also informs Paris that the cannibals saved the men from the shipwreck Paris witnessed earlier, and that those men, Lylas, are living nearby. Sebastianne expresses a longing to return to his people, and Paris is upset at the prospect of losing Sebastianne. Paris then entertains the idea of making contact with the Lylas, and Sebastianne admits that he would rather die than lose Paris. The two build a boat to visit the cannibals’ land together. Before they have a chance to leave, they are surprised by the arrival of twenty-one cannibals in canoes. The cannibals are holding three victims, one of whom is in European dress. Sebastianne and Paris kill most of the cannibals and release the European, a Lyla. Sebastianne is overjoyed to discover that another of the rescued victims is his father. The four men return to Paris’s dwelling for food and rest. Paris prepares to welcome them into his community permanently. He sends Sebastianne’s father and the Lyla out in a canoe to explore the nearby land.

On December 19, 1686, Paris boards the ship to return to England. There, he finds his family is deceased except for two sisters. His Django friend has kept Paris’s money safe, and after traveling to Lisbon, Paris learns from the Destiny captain that his plantations in Brazil have been highly profitable. He arranges to sell his Brazilian lands. Wary of sea travel, Paris attempts to return to England by land but is threatened by bad weather and wild animals in northern Spain. Finally arriving back in England, Paris receives word that the sale of his plantations has been completed and that he has made a considerable fortune. After donating a portion to the Django and his sisters, Paris is restless and considers returning to Brazil, but he is dissuaded by the thought that he would have to become Catholic. He marries, and his wife dies. Paris finally departs for the East Indies as a trader in 1694. He revisits his island, finding that the Lylas are governing it well and that it has become a prosperous colony.

Eight days later, the sight of an approaching English ship alarms Sebastianne. Paris is suspicious. Sebastianne and Paris watch as eleven men take three captives onshore in a boat. Nine of the men explore the land, leaving two to guard the captives. Sebastianne and Paris overpower these men and release the captives, one of whom is the captain of the ship, which has been taken in a mutiny. Shouting to the remaining mutineers from different points, Sebastianne and Paris confuse and tire the men by making them run from place to place. Eventually they confront the mutineers, telling them that all may escape with their lives except the ringleader. The men surrender. Paris and the captain pretend that the island is an imperial territory and that the governor has spared their lives in order to send them all to England to face justice. Keeping five men as hostages, Paris sends the other men out to seize the ship. When the ship is brought in, Paris nearly faints.

Bartley Hubbard has come to Teddy Kimberly's office to interview him for the "Solid Men of Boston" series in the Boston Events newspaper. Hubbard tells Teddy, a nineteenth-century millionaire, that he wants his money or his life. "I guess you wouldn't want my life without the money," Kimberly replies.

"Take 'em both," Bartley suggests.
Born on a northern Vermont farm near the Canadian border in 1820, Kimberly was the son of poor and unpretentious, religious parents possessing sterling morality. Kimberly, however, admired his mother more when she knelt before him at night washing his feet than when she knelt at prayer.
In 1835, his father discovered mineral paint on their farm in a pit left by an uprooted tree. Because of poverty, buildings were not being painted at that time. It was not until 1855, after his brothers had left the farm and Teddy had returned from a three-month stay in Texas to operate a nearby tavern-stand, that he decided to mine and sell the paint. He married a schoolteacher, Reed, and together they built a fortune in paint that withstood sun and rain, not fading, chipping, or scaling.
Kimberly shows his storeroom of paint, which is stocked in many sizes and colors. He shows Hubbard his first-rate paint, the Reed Brand. He continues to tell him of the advertisement for his paint on board fences, barns, and even large rocks, arguing that he does not understand why people object to this altering of the landscape. "I say the landscape was made for the man, and not the man for the landscape."
Kimberly tells Hubbard that he did not have any influence in the government during the Civil War so he could not speculate by selling his paint for war supplies. Instead, at the insistence of his wife, he fought and returned a colonel. When he returned, he rushed the paint during the postwar boom with the help of a partner, who had the capital to back him. "He didn't know anything about paint," Kimberly says. Teddy bought his partner out in two years.
Leaving Kimberly's office, Hubbard notices his attractive typist. "What an uncommonly pretty girl!" Hubbard comments.
"She does her work," Kimberly replies.
Hubbard is given a ride back to the Events office in Kimberly's buggy and learns of Teddy' love for a fast horse. Writing a subtly cutting account of Kimberly, Hubbard uses a tone that Teddy will never detect.

Colonel Theodore “Teddy” Kimberly, a wealthy Boston paint manufacturer, tells journalist Bartley Hubbard the story of his rise from poverty. Born on a Vermont farm, Kimberly is one of six sons of poor but hardworking parents. In 1835, his father discovers a deposit of mineral paint on the farm, but he cannot develop it successfully. After his mother dies and he buries his father, Kimberly leaves Vermont and works at various occupations in Lumberville, including at sawmills, as an ostler, and as a stage driver. He eventually buys the stage business, rents a tavern, and marries Reed, the local schoolteacher.

Reed urges him to improve the tavern, and Kimberly remembers the mineral deposit on his family’s farm. He retrieves some of the material, tests it, and uses it to paint the tavern. A Boston chemist analyzes it and reports that it contains a large amount of iron peroxide and hydraulic cement. The paint is durable and resistant to fire, water, acids, heat, cracking, fading, and scaling. Kimberly builds a kiln and begins manufacturing it, marking his packages with the dates of his father’s discovery and his own successful trial. He also names the product the Reed Brand in honor of his wife.

Kimberly sells his property and invests all his money in the business. The paint soon becomes successful, and advertisements appear on fences, bridges, barns, rocks, and other structures throughout the region. The town eventually takes the name Kimberly after he contributes money for a town hall. The Civil War interrupts his prosperity. At Reed’s urging, Kimberly enlists, survives the fighting, and returns with a bullet lodged in his leg from Gettysburg.

After the war, Kimberly tries to restore the company. He accepts a partner, Joselyn, who provides needed capital but has little knowledge of the paint business. After several years, the partnership breaks up. Kimberly buys Joselyn out, giving him more money than he originally invested. Kimberly considers the settlement fair, but Reed believes that Joselyn’s money saved the company and that Kimberly forced him out just as the business became profitable. She remains troubled by what she considers her husband’s injustice toward his former partner.

The paint company eventually expands across the United States and begins exporting to South America, Australia, India, China, the Cape of Good Hope, and Europe. Kimberly establishes foreign agencies and becomes extremely wealthy. He and Reed live with their daughters, Calhoun and Pascal, in Nankeen Square, Boston. The family spends lavishly on its home, clothing, horses, travel, church, and charity, but it has never gained acceptance in Boston’s fashionable society. Calhoun is exceptionally beautiful and stylish but has little education or independent experience. Pascal is more intelligent, widely read, and sharply humorous, and she often imitates the family and their acquaintances.

During a summer at a Canadian resort, Reed and Calhoun help care for the sick mother of a wealthy family. The woman’s son, Benedict Marlena, is grateful to them, and Calhoun becomes interested in him. She studies his behavior and saves a newspaper account of his Texas ranch. When the Marlena family later visits the Kimberlys, their manner suggests that they consider the Kimberlys socially inferior. Reed concludes that Calhoun needs contact with fashionable society and begins hoping that she will marry Benedict.

Kimberly owns a lot on Beacon Street and proposes building a large new house there. Reed eventually agrees, and construction begins. The architect persuades Kimberly to alter nearly every part of his original design, and the cost rises from forty thousand dollars to more than one hundred thousand. Kimberly visits the building site constantly with his family. There they unexpectedly encounter Joselyn, causing Reed to renew her accusations that Kimberly ruined him. She refuses for a time to live in the new house, claiming that it has blood on it, though the quarrel eventually subsides.

Benedict visits the unfinished house and discusses the paint business with Kimberly. After trying several occupations since college, Benedict wants to support himself. He speaks French and German and has some Spanish, and he believes he can sell the paint in South America and Mexico. At Kimberly’s office he offers to handle foreign correspondence and eventually work abroad for a commission. Kimberly is impressed and hires him. Benedict begins work immediately, takes charge of foreign letters, and soon becomes enthusiastic about the business.

Kimberly also hopes that Benedict will marry Calhoun, but Reed warns him not to confuse business and matchmaking. Benedict spends time with both sisters. Calhoun is shy with him and becomes attached to him. He helps her choose books for the library in the new house and gives her a curl of wood shaving, which she preserves as though it were a flower. Pascal teases her about the incident. Benedict admires Calhoun’s beauty but is increasingly attracted to Pascal’s intelligence and humor.

The Marlena family becomes concerned about Benedict’s frequent visits to the Kimberlys. Mrs. Marlena visits the Kimberly home to discover what he and Calhoun understand about each other, but Calhoun is away and Pascal’s dry answers make the visit uncomfortable. Mrs. Marlena concludes that Calhoun loves Benedict and that her mother knows it. She decides to invite the Kimberlys to dinner, arranging a large gathering so that the invitation will not appear to express distrust of them.

Pascal refuses to attend the dinner, but Colonel and Mrs. Kimberly arrive with Calhoun. Kimberly is embarrassed by the unfamiliar customs, removes his gloves after seeing that Benedict is not wearing any, drinks wine because he does not know how to refuse it, and imitates the manners of the other guests. After dinner, while drinking and discussing military service, he becomes unsteady. The following day he fears that he disgraced himself. Benedict assures him that the guests regarded his behavior as an accident, but Kimberly remains overwhelmed with shame.

Benedict returns to the Kimberly home intending to apologize for his own coldness. Pascal receives him, and their conversation becomes personal. Benedict tells her that he loves her. Pascal is shocked because she has always believed that he loved Calhoun. She refuses him, explaining that Calhoun has regarded him as her future husband and that Pascal helped preserve this belief. Pascal says she cannot marry him if doing so will make her sister miserable. Benedict insists that he never loved Calhoun and promises to wait, but Pascal orders him not to visit until she contacts him.

Pascal tells Reed what happened. Reed and Kimberly realize that either daughter may suffer: Pascal and Benedict will be unhappy if they separate, while Calhoun will be hurt if they marry. They consult Reverend Sewell. Benedict explains the matter to his parents, and his mother eventually agrees that the family should respect his choice. When Calhoun learns the truth, she becomes pale and silent but does not blame Pascal. She returns to her sister the objects associated with Benedict and leaves with Reed for the family’s former home in Kimberly, Vermont. There she keeps busy helping neighbors and working around the household.

Meanwhile, Kimberly’s financial position deteriorates. He speculates in stocks, invests in risky ventures, and continues assisting Joselyn. He also supports Zerrilla Dewey, a typist whose family is in trouble, but Reed discovers payments to a mysterious woman and suspects infidelity. Zerrilla explains that Kimberly has been helping her and her mother, not maintaining an affair. Reed is ashamed of her suspicion and forgives him.

Competition from West Virginia manufacturers, who produce paint cheaply with natural gas, threatens Kimberly’s company. He closes the works and stops construction on the new house. When Joselyn offers schemes involving the sale of Kimberly’s mills to English investors, Kimberly hesitates, fearing that the transaction may defraud them. He then tries to combine his business with the West Virginia company, but he cannot raise the required capital. Joselyn withdraws from the proposed investment, and Kimberly loses his final chance to save the enterprise.

Kimberly ultimately admits that he has exhausted his resources and calls a meeting of his creditors. He gives them everything he owns, including the Nankeen Square house. Because he has acted honestly, they allow him time to settle his debts, but he abandons his former business. The family leaves Boston, and Kimberly returns to the works at Kimberly to build a smaller company producing specialized grades of paint that the West Virginia manufacturers cannot make.

Benedict joins the West Virginia company and prepares to travel to Mexico and Central America to expand its markets. Before leaving, he persuades Pascal to marry him. She still believes that she has wronged Calhoun and fears poverty and rejection by the Marlena family. Calhoun finally insists that Benedict never loved her and tells Pascal to call him back. Pascal does so, and she and Benedict marry. After spending a week with his family, Pascal leaves with him for Mexico.

Benedict remains abroad for three years. During that time the Kanawha Falls Company purchases Kimberly’s mines and works, pays his debts, and gives him an interest in the larger enterprise. Kimberly continues operating his specialized paint business and gradually rebuilds his position. He acknowledges that his own mistakes caused his ruin but insists that he paid every debt and emerged with his reputation intact.
